title: The Sacred Flame
subtitle: The Vesperian communion of the First Light
summary: Every thinking person carries a Spark: Vespara, Talien and Marenne, the Crownless God, the Ashen King, and why a thousand flames are safer than one.
content:
> *"One flame lights another and loses nothing."*
> — Vesperian saying

The **Sacred Flame** is the Vesperian communion of the [[faith-of-the-first-light|Faith of the First Light]], and the dominant religious tradition of the [Vesper Republic](factions.html#vesper-republic). It shares its ancient roots with the Aurelian [[crowned-sun|Crowned Sun]]: both begin with **Light** appearing in primordial darkness and making things comprehensible, among them thought, distinction, possibility and responsibility.

Where the Crowned Sun reads that Light as revealing the proper order of things, the Sacred Flame reads it as something given to each person to use. Its emphases are **conscience**, **inquiry**, **creation**, **liberty** and **individual judgment**.

The Sacred Flame lives in a country that has also produced a great many secular citizens, rationalists and atheists, and it has learned to share its symbols with them. Plenty of Vesperians who would never call themselves religious still light a lamp before starting something important.

## The Spark

At the heart of the Sacred Flame is the teaching that every thinking person carries a portion of the First Light: **the Spark**.

No single person holds all of the truth. Not a king, not a priest, not a philosopher, not a government, not a university. Every person therefore has both the *ability* and the *responsibility* to think and to judge.

It is not hard to see why this theology suits Vesperian politics. A faith that says truth is distributed among everyone makes it difficult for anyone to claim to be beyond question, and Vesperians have never been shy about pointing that out to those who try.

## One Flame Lights Another

The communion's best-known phrase, *one flame lights another and loses nothing*, is used everywhere knowledge or help passes between people: teaching, publishing, education, mentorship, research and mutual aid.

It is also the root of the Vesperian hostility to monopolies over knowledge, and it is why arguments about dangerous Gate research in Vesper are never only political. They are theological too. If lighting another's flame costs nothing, what is the justification for keeping yours to yourself?

## Vespara, Bearer of Dawn

**Vespara** is associated with hope, beginnings, inspiration, rebellion, creativity and the conviction that things can be different. Her sentiment is three words long, and many Vesperians can recite nothing else of her teaching:

> *It could be otherwise.*

Vespara may descend from an older Lantern-Bearer shared across the First Light tradition, but what that older figure was like is not known. Aurelia honours her as a relatively minor figure of dawn, inspiration and improvement. Vesper raises her much higher. In the modern republican reading, she stands for the moral legitimacy of imagining a different order, which is to say, for the Revolution.

## Talien, Maker of Questions

**Talien** is the patron of scholars, inventors, philosophers, teachers, children and anyone who questions assumptions. Talien embodies inquiry, and the most important thing Talien's tradition teaches is that *asking a question is not, in itself, an act of disobedience*. Questions are how the Spark is exercised.

Talien belongs naturally in schools, universities, scientific societies and laboratories. The myths told about Talien have never been gathered into a settled form, and Vesperians tend to think that suits the Maker of Questions.

> **In a district schoolroom**
>
> The lesson was on the Charter of Citizens. A girl in the second row put up her hand.
>
> "If the Charter can be changed whenever enough people vote for it, couldn't enough people vote to get rid of the Charter?"
>
> The room went very quiet. Several children looked at the teacher to see how much trouble the girl was in.
>
> The teacher put down her chalk and smiled.
>
> "That," she said, "is the best question anyone has asked in this room all year. Talien would be proud of you. Now. Everyone take out a sheet of paper, because we are going to spend the rest of the afternoon trying to answer it."

## Marenne of the Open Door

**Marenne** is the patron of hospitality, mutual aid, refugees, solidarity, mercy and shelter. She stands for something the Sacred Flame insists on as firmly as it insists on liberty: freedom is not merely being left alone. **People have obligations to one another.**

Marenne keeps Vesperian faith from becoming purely individual. Her tradition is at home in refugee support, mutual-aid societies, neighbourhood organisations and labour solidarity. Her detailed myths are not settled; her open door is.

> **The night the river rose, as a neighbour remembered it**
>
> The Ninth Ward Residents' Committee had been meeting to argue about the tram timetable when the first family knocked on the hall door, soaked to the waist.
>
> Nobody called a vote. The chairman simply stopped talking. Someone pushed the long table against the wall. Someone else went home and came back with blankets. By midnight there were forty people sleeping on the floor of the hall, and the committee was taking turns at the stove.
>
> In the morning, somebody had chalked a small open door above the entrance. Nobody admitted to it.
>
> The tram timetable was resolved the following month, in favour of the motion.

## The Crownless God and the Ashen King

Two older mythic figures matter enormously to modern Vesper.

The **Crownless God** wanders, refuses kingship and resists every attempt at enthronement. Modern Vesperians read the Crownless God as a figure of anti-authoritarianism, of refusing domination, of legitimacy without crowns. What the story meant before the Revolution is not known. It would be a mistake to assume it was always republican; it may well have meant something quite different, and the Republic has every reason to read it the way it does.

The **Ashen King** is a warning. In the central version of the story, a ruler tries to gather or control every flame in his realm. There must be one approved flame, one source of light, one authorised truth. He puts out all the others. Then, one day, the central flame goes out, and because every other flame has been extinguished, the whole realm falls into darkness.

The lesson, in the Vesperian reading, is short:

> *A thousand flames are safer than one.*

The Ashen King may descend from the same older material as the Aurelian **Shadow Behind the Crown**, which teaches that rulers fail when authority is separated from responsibility. Vesperians say he fails because he tried to monopolise everyone else's light. No original shared version of the story has been recovered, and neither communion's reading can claim to be the historical one (see [[faith-of-the-first-light|The Faith of the First Light]]).

> **The Ashen King, as told to children at bedtime**
>
> *...and the King said, "Why should there be so many little lights, all flickering and arguing? I shall keep one great flame, and everyone shall come to me to see."*
>
> *So his soldiers went from house to house, and they put out every candle and every lamp and every hearth, and they brought the people to the palace to stand in the light of the great flame.*
>
> *And one night, there was a wind.*
>
> *"What happened?" asks the child, who always asks, though she knows.*
>
> *"It went out," says her father. "And there was nobody left who had a light to give him."*
>
> *"So what's the lesson?"*
>
> *"A thousand flames are safer than one. Now go to sleep. And leave your lamp alone."*

## Revolution and Religion

The Revolution did not abolish religion, but it split it. Some clergy supported the monarchy, opposed the Revolution or fled. Others supported reform, joined revolutionary movements and reinterpreted scripture in their light. At various points, revolutionary governments tried to replace or subordinate older religious practice with civic ceremonies, secular festivals and revolutionary symbols.

Over time, faith and republican politics adapted to each other. Modern Vesper includes committed Sacred Flame believers, secular citizens, rationalists, atheists and a great many people who keep religious customs without strong belief. Religious freedom and the separation of church and state sit far more comfortably in today's Republic than a state church ever could. How exactly the law came to be arranged that way is a story the Archive has not yet recorded in full.

> **Two priests, one text, during the Year of Ash (as later recounted by both their congregations)**
>
> The text was an old one: *"Keep the flame that is given to you."*
>
> The royalist priest preached it on the cathedral steps. "Keep it. Guard what has been entrusted to you. The order you were born into is a flame too, and you were given it to tend, not to set fire to the house with."
>
> Across the square, from the back of a cart, the republican priest preached the same words. "Keep it. *Your* flame. Not the King's, not the bishop's, not mine. It was given to you, and nobody may take it into custody on your behalf."
>
> Both of them, their congregations insist, were quoting it correctly.

## Death and the Returning Spark

Vesperian teaching holds that the Spark does not simply vanish at death. One widely held interpretation says that it returns to the greater First Flame. Just as importantly, a person continues through their ideas, their students, their works and inventions, and the people they changed.

The best-known Vesperian funeral custom expresses this directly: a flame is lit for the dead and then passed into several smaller candles held by the mourners. One life, continuing through many others. What happens to the Spark beyond that, and whether anything of the person remains as a person, is a question the Sacred Flame has left open.

## Customs

Many Sacred Flame practices sit somewhere between formal religion, popular custom and civic habit, and vary by region and family. Among the most common:

- **lighting a lamp** when beginning an important project;
- **passing a flame** between friends before a long separation;
- **leaving a light burning** for someone who is expected to return;
- **sharing the funeral flame** among the mourners;
- **burning written grievances**, or old commitments, during festivals, as a way of letting them go.

There is no single universal liturgy that every Vesperian keeps, and the Sacred Flame has never seemed troubled by that.

## The Flame and the Gates

The Gates caused far less theological alarm in Vesper than in Aurelia. Most Vesperian believers met them with fascination. Three ideas dominate the discussion:

- **The Infinite Flame.** If thinking beings exist beyond the Gates, perhaps the First Light is not limited to the known world, and those beings carry Sparks of their own. For many Vesperians this is a thrilling thought: reason and consciousness might be universal.
- **The Stolen Flame.** Some theologians and ethicists ask whether taking a Gate's Core removes something essential from another world. Nobody knows what Cores are, and the Sacred Flame has not decided. The question is asked seriously, and it has been asked more urgently ever since the first Core was brought home and its Gate closed behind it.
- **Knowledge as Light.** Vesperians naturally treat Gate research as illumination, which makes any attempt to censor it feel close to blasphemy. But Vesper also remembers the [[the-vesper-republic|Open Archive Incident]]. *Spreading light can also start fires*, and the most thoughtful Vesperian believers keep both halves of that sentence in view.
